name: Zearn
line: Zearn's unit is a lesson, checked by a quiz at its end. In AMP, the problem is the unit, and assessment is continuous.
description: AMP vs Zearn: Zearn moves through grade-level lessons in order, each ending in a quiz. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: By default, Zearn moves a student through one grade's lessons in a fixed order, and each lesson ends in a quiz that must be passed to open the next [1]. In AMP, assessment is continuous: every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem. Each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer, and learned skills keep returning in practice.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Zearn has no placement test. By default, a student starts at Mission 1, Lesson 1 of the assigned grade and moves through the lessons in order. A teacher can move a student elsewhere in the kindergarten to grade 8 lessons [1]. Its check comes once in each lesson, in the quiz at the end [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem in front of the learner: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Zearn the unit is the lesson, about 30 minutes long: a fluency warm-up, short videos with on-screen teachers that pause for the student to solve problems, then the Tower of Power quiz [1][3][5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [15].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. In Zearn a student works in one grade's lessons, and the teacher assigns each unit to match class instruction [1][4]. Its lessons cover kindergarten through grade 8 [3][10].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a learner shows a skill by getting it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on, while every other part of math stays at its own level. Zearn keeps students in grade-level lessons by design and gives help for a gap inside the lesson, rather than moving a student back to an earlier grade's lessons [8][9]. Its own observational study of 600,000 students found less struggle on the next lesson this way [9]. A teacher can assign recommended foundational lessons [6], and Zearn advises teachers to move all students to the next unit with whole-class teaching, whether or not they have finished every lesson [1].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Zearn checks each lesson once, with the quiz at its end, and a score of 100% opens the next lesson [1]. We found no scheduled review of earlier lessons on the Zearn pages that describe its lessons [3][4]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8, one grade's lessons at a time [3][10][1].
rows.start: No placement test. By default, a student starts at Mission 1, Lesson 1 of the assigned grade. A teacher can reassign [1].
rows.teaching: Lessons of about 30 minutes: a fluency warm-up, then short videos with on-screen teachers that pause for the student to solve problems, on screen and on paper [3][4][5].
rows.next: The next lesson in a fixed order. Teachers assign units and can assign recommended foundational lessons [1][6].
rows.mastery: 100% on the lesson's Tower of Power quiz, with unlimited attempts, opens the next lesson [1].
rows.review: None found in the pages we read [3][4].
rows.print: Printable student and teacher materials [6]. Printed books for each grade, the same for every student in it [11].
rows.adult: Assigns units, watches live reports and alerts, assigns foundational lessons, and in the intended model teaches the lesson [4][7][6].
rows.reports: Who is working and who is stuck, progress toward grade-level goals, pace reports, and alerts when a student struggles on a quiz [4][6].
rows.evidence: Independent randomized trial: state test +0.07 SD, not significant; MAP +0.11, exploratory [1]. Rated Strong by Evidence for ESSA [2].

theirs: Zearn Math's lessons cover kindergarten through grade 8 [3]. The kindergarten to grade 5 lessons derive from Eureka Math under license from Great Minds, and grades 6 to 8 from Open Up Resources' middle school math [12]. Zearn says the program is designed to complement teacher-led instruction [7].

A teacher assigns a Mission, a unit that matches class instruction, and students work through its lessons in order [4]. A lesson takes about 30 minutes [5]. It opens with fluency activities. Then come short videos with on-screen teachers that pause for the student to solve problems, on screen and on paper [1][3]. It closes with the Tower of Power, a quiz that needs 100% to open the next lesson [1].
credit: Grade-level lessons built on Eureka Math and Open Up Resources' middle school math [12].
Work on paper in every lesson, beside the work on screen [3].
A large randomized trial, run by researchers outside the company [1].

theirs: Zearn's strongest evidence is an independent randomized trial. RAND researchers, funded by the U.S. Institute of Education Sciences, randomly assigned 64 schools in a large Texas district, with more than 10,000 students in grades 3 to 5, and followed them for two years [1]. Zearn helped design the study and supplied teacher training, coaching and prize challenges. Control schools kept their usual programs, which included other math software. After two years the effect on the state STAAR test was +0.07 standard deviations, positive but not statistically significant. On the MAP test it was +0.11, significant but labeled exploratory. In the first year 18% of students reached the goal of 90 lessons; in the second year 50% did [1].

Evidence for ESSA rates Zearn Math Strong, based on three studies including one randomized trial, with an average effect size of +0.09 [2]. The other two are Johns Hopkins matched comparisons. In Louisiana, in a study run with Zearn and funded by Accelerate, students in three districts using Zearn with coaching scored +0.20 standard deviations higher on the state test than matched students in districts averaging under one Zearn lesson a week. Against districts Zearn picked as planning a full rollout, the difference was +0.09, not significant [13]. A 2019 study of 15 schools found no significant difference overall [2][1].

Zearn's larger figures, such as users growing state scores 2.5 times more than matched students, come from its own studies [6]. These compare students who met a usage target, such as three lessons a week, with matched students who did not [5][1]. RAND's researchers say such estimates are likely biased upward [1]. RAND also reports that, as of April 2025, the What Works Clearinghouse had not reviewed any study of Zearn Math [1].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, practice that mixed and spaced topics scored 62% a month later, against 38% for practice in blocks [14]. The test was the researchers' own. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [15]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want a class to work through the same grade-level lessons in order, beside the teacher's own lessons.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or past grade 8.
You want the adult free of planning, teaching and grading.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Zearn?
questions.answer: Zearn moves a student through one grade's lessons in order, and each lesson ends in a quiz that opens the next [1]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Zearn work?
questions.answer: In RAND's randomized trial of more than 10,000 Texas students, the two-year effect on the state test was +0.07 standard deviations, not statistically significant, and +0.11 on the MAP test, an exploratory result [1]. Evidence for ESSA rates Zearn Math Strong [2]. Zearn's larger figures come from comparing students who met a usage target with matched students who did not [5].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers and chooses practice from there.
